Faisal Islam: This Budget was micro and that was deliberate
text:
It was not a mini Budget, but it was rather small. It might be called the "micro Budget".

Small does not necessarily mean bad, but it clearly falls short of radical action to create a promised new economic model.

A new "theory of growth" was not unveiled as promised by the prime minister Andy Burnham.

It was preamble, roadmap, consultation, perhaps the starter to the main course, which appears to be the PM's 10-year plan next month.

It went unsaid, but the clear stategic aim of Healey's statement was to be the "anti-mini Budget".

This "steady as she goes" predictable fiscal event set out to avoid the aftermath seen following Liz Truss's mini-budget, in which unexpected and unfunded tax cuts spooked the bond and currency markets.

The markets didn't even flicker on Healey's announcement of £65bn of extra borrowing over the next five years - government interest costs have actually fallen since Wednesday, against the backdrop of market turmoil due to the US-Iran war.

The core of the Budget was to get Downing Street through the impacts of the Middle East conflict shock on energy and borrowing costs.

If these pressures prove enduring there are some unpalatable decisions that will have to be grasped within the next year. The can will have to be picked up rather than kicked down the road again.

It buys more time, more "breathing space", as it were, for the government and the prime minister's long-term strategic plans.

The detail may come more quickly than feared. On welfare, the Milburn Review process is clearly heading for some sort of welfare-to-work scheme, even a separate system for younger workers.

It will cost money up front to subsidise work opportunities and hope to save more from welfare bills in the future. The chancellor saw at close quarters Gordon Brown do this twice two decades ago.

The Office for Budget Responsbility's (OBR) economic forecast showed the sheer rise in the welfare bill, which is set to jump to £431bn in 2031, if pensioner support is included.

There are two further areas where the chancellor laid down markers, with little fiscal cost, in terms of the long term plan.

On energy, there is some significance to the "cheaper power" mission announced, reshaping what had previously been a focus on clean power.

While still committed to Net Zero, a series of technical changes to powers over levies and renewable auctions, will seek to turn the tide on additional pressures on energy costs.

On devolution, the plan to allow local mayors to keep some extra business rate and income tax revenues, are more radical than expected.

There are trade offs here, but it essentially provides incentives for regional leaders to grow their economies, workforce and tax base, that are normal elsewhere, but have not existed in the UK's very centralised tax system.

How the PM will square other aspects of his "theory of growth" with the chancellor's spending constraints is the other significant challenge.

Can he announce a 10-year plan without detailing the Liverpool to Manchester high speed train line, or a rebirth of some cancelled HS2 lines he championed a year ago?

Away from the long term, the OBR forecast point to a very tricky economic backdrop until the spring, and a trickier spending review, given the need to accommodate the new defence target of 3% of national income by 2030.

The PM's insistence he will not call an election for a year are eminently believable given the risk of 5% inflation and declining household income.

A "focused" Budget at an uncertain time achieved its narrow aim of a bit of "breathing space" for households and also for the government itself.

But the evident gaps in the Budget will need filling in come the PM's upcoming 10-year plan.

title: Best mountain bike lights 2026: Top MTB lights reviewed and rated by our expert off-road testers
author: Guy Kesteven
text:
Why are you wasting hours of potential riding fun in winter when the best mountain bike lights mean you can ride the rowdiest trails right through to dawn?

Even affordable mountain bike lights are bright enough to push the pace on tasty trails for an hour or more, while more expensive sets will give near daylight conditions for several hours. Helmet lights put their power exactly where you look, so even the tightest corners or steepest drops don't catch you out.

Even so, riding at night will put a whole new spin on your rides, with everything seeming faster and totally fresh – even on local trails you ride day after day. As well as being huge fun, night riding is a great way to maintain hard-won summer fitness into the new year.

The great news is that after huge advances in lithium-ion battery, LED and display tech, light development has slowed down recently. That means proven, reliable designs at every price point, rather than troublesome tech that's been rushed into the after-dark arms race.

So scroll down our list of the best mountain bike handlebar and helmet lights from under £100 to over £500 to find the perfect products for taking your XC, trail, enduro and riding 24/7. If you want to check out our pick of models better suited for on-road use, see our guide to the best bike lights .

A big can of British night beating tech

6,000 (in Reflex mode) | 411g / 14.5oz | 20,000mAh | IP67 (dust-tight, fully submersible in water up to 1m) | USB-C | Min run time (triple tested): 2hrs 10mins

Super sturdy, weatherproof design

7 pre-programmed settings with run times up to 36hrs

Can use the light as a power bank

Mounting shoe bolt can rattle loose

✅ You want massive wireless power: Self-contained design means no cables or separate batteries to worry about. Excellent product support: Exposure is legendary for looking after their customers with excellent warranty and repair cover.

❌ You want max power for price: Clever tech and UK build means high price for the lumen count.

❌ You don't like fussy mounts: Mount and light bolt tensioning are a torque tightrope.

Exposure incrementally improves its lights on a regular basis, and its latest Six Pack Mk15 is its most powerful front light yet - but that's not the biggest news.

The Six Pack now has a maximum output of 6,000 lumens (peak power in Reflex mode) from six white XPL2 (W3) LEDs powered by an internal 20,000 mAH Li-Ion battery that's 17.6% bigger than the last model. The run time ranges from just over two hours to a day and half, depending on which of the seven pre-programmed settings are selected.

Three of those programs use Exposure's Reflex 2.0 technology, which uses onboard accelerometers to calculate when you’re riding downhill or rough terrain and will automatically boost the light's output to max. It will then automatically go back to its regular output when things calm down and dim significantly if you stop.

Self-rationing run times are also slightly easier on the Mk15 thanks to a new colour OLED screen on the back of the light (previous versions had a monotone LED display). The displayed run times (Reflex is by its nature something of a lottery) are actually accurate too, which isn't always the case with other lights. The screen background colour also changes 'traffic light style' as your remaining runtime ticks down.

The big practical news for this update is that the SixPack 15 swaps its bespoke charger and plug design for USB-C. That means it can be fast-charged (minimum claimed time is five hours) from any appropriate socket/plug setup. The light can also be used as an emergency power bank for other USB-C devices.

Exposure has also introduced a new handlebar bracket. The hinged clamp with clip-in inserts for 31.8 or 35mm bars is definitely easier to fit than the previous jigsaw design, and the forward-projecting arm that holds the light is longer for improved clearance on crowded bars. Our test sample had wobble in the projecting arm bolt to start with, but that was sorted by tightening to the maximum torque of 6Nm (it's not marked on the clamp, but we checked with Exposure). Both the steel arm and bar band bolts screw into alloy threads, so be sure to use a torque wrench so you don't strip the threads.

Other mounting options come in the form of stem bolt and GoPro-style mounts available separately from Exposure, but the sheer bulk of the Six Pack means they won't work on some bikes. Whatever mount you choose, the triangular shoe on the underside of the light that engages with the QR mount is a potential weak link. The connection is again a short steel bolt into alloy threads. That creates another torque tightrope between security and stripping, and we'd advise regular checks that it's tight.

Mounting issues aside, the light output from the multiple LED's is excellent with the Six Pack's seven preset programs. Program 1 provides the brightest illumination and benefits from the Reflex 2.0 technology. The 4240-lumen output in the High setting is very impressive, providing a broad beam pattern to capture all the trail features directly in front of you. This gives at least 25 meters of illumination down the trail and a good spread to the sides. Once the onboard sensors have detected you’re heading downhill, the output seamlessly increases to the maximum 6,000 lumens. That's more than enough for most trails, though, so I generally run the light in lower power settings (Program 2 or 3) to avoid any run-time anxiety.

Exposure's quoted run times are actually around 10 percent short of what I got in testing. Even once the counter runs to zero, the Six Pack still gives 30 minutes of low-power 'Reserve' light to limp you home too.

The customer support from Exposure has a reputation for being equally helpful with reasonably priced repairs and spares, as well as a generous warranty program. I even know of several Exposure lights still in circulation literally decades after being bought, which is a big plus in terms of value.

There’s no avoiding the fact that the Six Pack is expensive, but the beam is outstanding for a self-contained light. The new screen and USB-C functionality are useful upgrades, and long-term customer support is top-class.

Premium lightweight UK made race light but not without niggles

2,650 (Reflex mode) | 222g / 7.8oz | 8,000mAh | IP67 (dust-tight, fully submersible in water up to 1m) | USB-C | Min run time (triple tested): 1hr 5mins

Great beam quality for speed

Useful screen and USB-C charging upgrades

Excellent customer service

Expensive for middling power

Beam too focused for tech trails

✅ You want a fancy, focused, lightweight light with lots of features: Great speed beam for the weight with new colour screen wins. You want excellent customer service: Exposure typically look after their products and buyers for decades.

❌ You want maximum lumens for your money: You can get the same peak and practical power much cheaper. You want 100% reliability on all features : My sample would get stuck in peak Reflex mode ruining battery runtimes.

The Race is a lightweight, focused beam light that has been in Exposure's range for decades. This Mk19 is the lightest (222g) and most compact (107mm long and 41mm in diameter at the bright end) version they've made. It still uses their trademark machined alloy cylinder design with carved ribs for cooling, two LEDs at the front and a new coloured OLED screen at the back. Exposure has also introduced USB-C charging on all their latest-generation lights and you get a high-quality fast charger included with the Race.

Peak output is 2,650 lumens in the brightest of the three automatic movement-sensing, self-dimming Reflex+ modes. That drops to 1,800 lumens in the brightest of the four manual modes. The relatively narrow 14-degree spot beam flatters those numbers in terms of distance you can see on simple, straight trails. The sharp cut-off and lack of peripheral coverage can get 'Blair Witch' very quickly on more twisty tech though. That means you'd be better off with the Toro, MaxxD, or the Six Pack (see above) for trail use.

While the brighter colours make reading runtimes easier, the OLED screen on the back of the light is still harder to see than a top-mounted screen. While it's hard to read the digits as you ride, you can't miss the background colour changing from green to yellow to red as your remaining runtime ticks down.

The Reflex+ mode on my sample light would only dim after being totally stationary for several minutes though, rather than when it sensed smoother/slower riding. That meant the claimed three-hour run time dropped dramatically to around an hour. I've had better luck with Reflex on other Exposure lights though, and Will didn't experience issues with his Race sample during testing.

I did have the same potential wobble and bolt-strip concerns with the new bar bracket with the Race as I did with the Six Pack. Although the much lighter weight of the Race means it's all stayed put OK so far.

Looking at the other options in this list from Lezyne, Ravemen and Magicshine will underline the Exposure price premium you're paying for a light that isn't perfect. They are made in the UK with a three-year warranty though. Plus, Exposure has an excellent reputation for repairing faulty lights or refreshing batteries, etc., at reasonable prices, even decades after they've been bought, which is worth factoring in when deciding which light to go for.

Outbound proves quality of light beats quantity on tech trails

2,200 | 276g / 9.7oz | 10,000mAh | IP65 (dust-tight and withstands low-pressure water jets) | USB-C | Min run time (triple tested): 1hr 45min

Excellent broad beam pattern

Low profile, centralised design

Very clever Adaptive Mode

Excellent reliability and warranty

Lots of custom mount options

Very expensive shipping outside USA

Basic battery communication

Switch can be hard to use in gloves

✅ You want excellent tech trail illumination: Multi LEDs and smart optics mean superb light quality for reading upcoming trouble.

✅ Excellent practical performance: Low-profile design, solid mount, excellent reliability and simple operation.

❌ You want max lumens for your money: Outbound concentrate on quality of light not quantity.

❌ You don't want to pay hefty import charges: Delivery charges are high outside the USA and there's currently no established UK distribution.

US firm Outbound Lighting is relatively new but is already floating on a raft of rave reviews from users. The Trail Evo is the flagship design of their 'broader is better' philosophy. Translating medium numbers on paper into outstanding night vision on the trail.

The secret lies in the nine double-row LEDs and broad, ribbed flood optic, which spreads light really well across the trail. The carefully curated (and extensively tested) multi-point light delivery means the 3D representation of the trail is excellent, rather than it being flattened by concentrated light.

While it's brighter in the centre for reasonable reach, it dims progressively to the periphery just as your own vision does, and the colour temperature is very natural too. There are no bright spots, dark spots, or other optical glitches to distort your read of the trail either. That all means that while the headline lumens are relatively low, the 'feels like riding in the day' result is outstanding, even compared to much brighter lights.

The transverse rather than inline (torch style) design mounts the battery across the back of the lights. Critically, they're separated by cooling airflow from a big chin scoop so the LEDs and battery stay efficient rather than cooking. Once you've got it bolted into place and learned the clip-in knack, the light is held centrally in front of the stem and it's totally wobble-free too. There's even an optional cable clip to make sure all your control lines stay out of the way under the light.…

title: Bereaved families will not face tax bill over pension delays under new rules
text:
Bereaved families will no longer be hit by an unexpected tax bill because of severe delays paying out civil service pensions, following a change in Wednesday's Budget.

Under previous HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments had to be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.

Campaigners had warned some families could face an unfair financial penalty because of delays which were not their fault.

The government has now changed the rules so payments will no longer become taxable solely because more than two years has passed.

The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.

Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.

Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.

Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.

According to the latest figures up to 30 September , external , 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.

The Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, previously said only a small number of these cases were approaching the two-year threshold.

However the PCS union, which represents civil servants, had warned there were "serious questions" over how long cases would remain unresolved.

Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss says

Emergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensions

Retired civil servants left in pension limbo

Rob Wassell, 58, had to wait more than two years following the death of his brother until he finally received the lump sum from his civil service pension on Tuesday.

After his case was highlighted by the BBC last week, Rob says he got a call from the pension scheme's complaints department who told him the payment was on its way.

However, because it was made after two years it was taxed at 45%, amounting to thousands of pounds.

If the payment was made after the rule change, it would not have been subject to tax.

Rob told the BBC he was pleased the government had addressed the issue in the Budget as this would mean others in his situation would not face a tax bill.

While he said he was happy to finally get his payment it was "a bitter pill to swallow" as he is now waiting for the outcome of a complaint review to find out if the tax will be reimbursed.

Rob said he was hopeful he would get the money back, adding: "I don't want to have to fight it anymore, it's been an ordeal already."

Pensions minister Torsten Bell confirmed the rule change in a letter to the chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee , external , Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who had raised concerns about the issue after it was highlighted by BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live programme.

Bell said the move would "make the position fairer for all grieving families and friends where there are delays in the payment of death benefits, whether in the Civil Service or any other pensions scheme".

He added: "Removing the tax deadline does not remove [a pension scheme's] wider duties to administer schemes prudently and without avoidable delay."

Under the previous rules, if someone died before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit was only tax-free if it was paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value was below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.

However, the government has now removed the two-year deadline so payments will no longer become taxable solely because they were made more than two years after a pension scheme was notified of the death.

The change applies to payments made from 28 October.

In his letter, the pensions minister said people who had already been impacted by avoidable delays and been taxed as a result could seek compensation through the pension scheme's complaints process and the Pensions Ombudsman.

Sir Geoffrey welcomed the announcement but said it does not "absolve Capita from processing and making payments to members of this scheme in a timely manner".

Fran Heathcote, general secretary of the PCS union, also welcomed the change but said "this situation should never have arisen in the first place".

She added: "Bereaved families must not pay the price for failures in the pension system.

"Capita is not off the hook, it continues to fail members and their families, which is why the scheme must be brought back in-house."

Capita has previously apologised for the impact of delays on pension scheme members and their families.

The company has said it is working to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with a particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging circumstances.

title: Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you
text:
Families facing cost-of-living pressures are being offered some help, or "breathing space" as Chancellor John Healey is calling it.

The help comes as prices are rising faster than expected with annual energy bills in particular likely to increase by hundreds of pounds in January.

Here's how the key announcements in the Budget affect you and your money.

If you are living in a home in council tax bands A to D in England, you will receive a one-off £100 "Household Energy Payment" from January, funded by extra tax on banks.

It will be paid directly into your bank account.

Council tax bands are listed below - you can check which one you are in by looking at your annual bill or checking the government's website , external , although that was struggling to cope with traffic after the announcement.

Administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive the equivalent funding, and they will decide whether to introduce the same payment.

This is designed to help with soaring energy bills, with some forecasts suggesting a typical annual bill could rise by £400 or so to £2,100 in January the saving will be only a portion of that. Although it's designated for energy bills, you can spend the money on anything you wish.

The VAT cut on electricity bills, which was introduced in October, will also be extended to July. It was due to end in April.

Healey announces £100 energy payment for millions and bank tax rise in first Budget

The fee for connecting to your gas supply so called standing charges will be scrapped in England, Scotland and Wales, next year "or as soon as possible after", the chancellor said.

These fixed daily charges will then be shifted onto the price you pay for each unit of energy.

The Treasury calculates that 60% of households will save an average of £45 a year, with lower users gaining the most. But the saving will come after the projected big rise in bills in January.

Higher users - in the biggest houses but also large, low-income families - will pay more than they currently do.

The government wants to extend reforms to electricity standing charges later.

The 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel, introduced by Rishi Sunak in 2022, will be extended to July. It was scheduled to be phased out from January.

It means drivers will still pay the levy at 52.95p per litre.

Motor fuel prices have risen sharply owing to the continued impact of the Iran war on drivers, with diesel having recently hit new records when it moved above £2 per litre.

The cost of filling a typical family car with diesel has gone up by around £30 since late February. A tankful of petrol costs about £23 more.

The chancellor has scrapped his predecessor's plans to reduce the annual amount people can save tax-free in cash in Individual Savings Accounts (Isas).

Rachel Reeves had wanted the policy to encourage personal investment in stocks and shares.

It meant, from April 2027, if you're under 65, you would only be able to save £12,000 a year in cash in an Isa, rather than £20,000.

Instead, the government plans to create a new "Starter Isa" for first-time investors.

If you have a large amount in savings, or if you fail to use the tax-free Isa allowance, then you will pay more tax from April.

You do not pay tax on all savings. There is the annual £20,000 Isa allowance, and an annual savings income allowance (in other words, the interest received on a savings pot) of £1,000 for basic rate taxpayers and £500 for higher-rate taxpayers.

But beyond that savings tax rates will rise by four percentage points to 24% and 44% respectively from April.

Landlords could also pay more in tax. In analysis published on Wednesday, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said these steps along with measures over the past decade that have reduced private landlord returns "collectively risk leading to a steady rise in rents".

Minimum wage rates will rise by 3.9% in April. It means:

Eligible workers aged 21 and over on the National Living Wage will receive £13.21 an hour, up from £12.71

If you are aged 18, 19 or 20, the National Minimum Wage will increase to £11.27 an hour, up from £10.85

For those aged 16 or 17, the minimum wage will rise to £8.31 an hour, up from £8

The separate apprentice rate which applies to eligible people under 19 - or those over 19 in the first year of an apprenticeship – will also increase to £8.31 an hour, from £8

However, these figures mean, this time around, there's no progress on Labour's manifesto promise to narrow the gap in minimum wages between older and younger workers.

For all workers, the ongoing freeze in the income bands , or thresholds, at which income tax is paid went unmentioned in the Budget.

But it means any kind of pay rise could drag you into a higher tax bracket, or see a greater proportion of your income taxed than would otherwise be expected. Scotland has its own income tax bands.

How much is the minimum wage going up by?

The triple lock policy means that the state pension will go up in line with average wage increases, at 3.9%.

the flat-rate state pension for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 will be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year, up £488 on now

the old basic state pension for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 will be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, up £374.40 on now

The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension.

The chancellor said this would be the case until at least 2030, as there will be a new Pension Tax Allowance, so pensioners with an income up to the value of the full new state pension will not pay income tax.

The First Time Buyer Isa has been in the planning stages with the government for a while.

Healey has confirmed that it is intended to replace the often-criticised Lifetime Isa.…

title: DoorDash to buy Instacart in $17bn deal it says will expand customer options
text:
DoorDash will acquire grocery delivery firm Instacart in a $17bn (£12.8bn) deal, creating a behemoth that will bring more meals, quick-need purchases and big weekly shops directly to customers.

DoorDash said the deal, expected to be final in about a year, will expand options for customers and let more sellers use the companies' services.

Instacart shoppers will be able to buy from 150,000 stores, up from the current 100,000, while DoorDash will reach beyond restaurants into retail, the firms said.

"Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve," Instacart's chief executive said.

"Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more," CEO Chris Rogers also said.

For DoorDash, the acquisition will allow it to use Instacart's grocery selection and substitution expertise, the company's co-founder and chief executive, Tony Xu, said.

"Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you'd choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts," Xu said.

He added that "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day".

The deal, expected to be done by the end of 2027 or first six months of 2028, is DoorDash's biggest acquisition to date, and could help it take on delivery giants like Amazon.

Morningstar analyst Martin Szumski told Reuters that the growth area in food delivery was shifting.

"Restaurant delivery is maturing, and growth now lies in more frequent, higher-value orders: weekly grocery shops, convenience items, and retail," he said.

In the agreement, DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a value of $65 a share, which would be a 26% premium on the closing price of Instacart stock on 22 October - the price before news of the potential merger first emerged. The deal will be at least 75% cash, DoorDash said.

DoorDash plans to keep Instacart's brand, app, and technology products. The delivery services will keep operating as independent companies until the deal is concluded.

The merger may raise antitrust issues with government regulators, Reuters also reported.

New York City's commission on consumer and worker protections, which last month reached a $131.5m settlement with DoorDash over allegations of underpaying workers, said in a statement: "This proposed merger continues a troubling trend of mega-corporations consolidating."

"Whether or not this merger proceeds, we will fully enforce delivery workers' rights," it added.

title: Tadej Pogačar and Demi Vollering top Vélo d'Or nominations – Who would get your vote?
author: Matilda Price
text:
A few days after Harry Kane and Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d'Or for excellence in football, the 2026 Vélo d'Or nominations were revealed with the season's biggest stars leading the shortlists for the men's and women's awards.

The Vélo d'Or – 'Golden Bicycle' in English – is a prestigious award that is handed out by France's with the winners decided by a jury of international cycling journalists.

There are two main awards, the Vélo d'Or for men and women, which is given to the overall best road rider of the year. There are then a number of sub-categories, including Classics rider of the year, sprinter of the year, rookie of the year, French rider of the year and paracyclist of the year.

The shortlists for all of the categories were unveiled on Thursday, a month ahead of the awards ceremony on Saturday, November 28, in Paris, with nominations full of the year's standout racers.

Three-time winner Tadej Pogačar is once again nominated for the men's award after taking his fifth Tour de France title, with his teammates Isaac del Toro and world champion Brandon McNulty also making the list. The two other Grand Tour winners of the year – Jonas Vingegaard and Enric Mas – also earned nominations, alongside Paul Seixas, Remco Evenepoel and Felix Gall.

Only two Classics specialists are up for the main award: Mathieu van der Poel and Wout van Aert.

On the women's list, Demi Vollering is surely a favourite to win her second Vélo d'Or, with last year's winner Pauline Ferrand-Prévot perhaps surprisingly not receiving a nomination after a lacklustre year on the road, though she is nominated for French rider of the year.

Tour de France Femmes stars Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, Marlen Reusser and Elisa Longo Borghini all make the list, as did revelation Paula Blasi, Antonia Niedermaier, Juliette Berthet, Anna van der Breggen, Kim Le Court-Pienaar and sprint sensation Lorena Wiebes.

Matthew Brennan, Jakob Omrzel and Paul Seixas are up for the men's rookie of the year, with Paula Blasi, Célia Gery and Isabella Holmgren earning the women's rookie nominations.

Whilst we won't know the official, jury-ratified results until the end of November, now that the nominations are out we wanted to put the shortlists to you and see who our readers would vote for.

Did Pogačar do enough to earn a fourth award, or has Paul Seixas run away with it? Can anyone come close to Demi Vollering's achievements this year? And which rookie impressed you?

title: Carrick keeps Fernandes as captain and says he needs no assurances on United future
author: Will Unwin
text:
Carrick says he is not surprised still to be head coach

He describes Fernandes as ‘important’ for the squad

Michael Carrick has said he will not strip Bruno Fernandes of the Manchester United captaincy after dropping him for the defeat by Bournemouth and that he is not surprised to have kept his job as the head coach.

Carrick and Fernandes held talks this week after the Portuguese criticised the tactics in the loss to Como, resulting in the midfielder being an unused substitute on Sunday. Harry Maguire took the armband but will not retain it for Saturday’s game at Chelsea, with Carrick saying “there is no decision to be made” and praising Fernandes.

“He’s an important player for this group,” he said. “He has been and he will be. Between us, we’ve got to make a difference and we’ve got to push things in a good direction. He’s fully committed to this football club, he’s fully committed to making things better. It doesn’t change for me. He’s the one that’s kind of led the team so well for many a game and many a year, and he’ll continue to do that.”

Carrick’s future remains unclear but he has been given a chance to turn around United’s form. The hierarchy held talks over whether to stick with Carrick at the start of the week after eight games without a win, including a wait of more than two months for a Premier League victory. There is keen interest in Eddie Howe or Julian Nagelsmann as potential replacements.

“I don’t need any assurances from anyone,” Carrick said. “I totally get the position, I understand the job, I understand the responsibilities, I understand what comes with that.”

Asked whether he was surprised still to be in charge, Carrick said: “No, I am here to do my job. I am here to do the best for the team, and I am desperate to make us better and improve things, so I’m not surprised, no.”

The United supporters cheered Carrick off after the Bournemouth game, turning their anger on the players, who were booed at Old Trafford. “I care about what the supporters think,” Carrick said. “I care about what it feels like in the stadium, and them travelling for games, to come and see us and support us.

“I care about what we give them, and what we offer them, and what they see. I genuinely don’t take any notice of anything else. I know this job, I know what it brings, I know what we need to do really to be better. I don’t need anyone else to tell me anything else.”

United will be without the striker Benjamin Sesko until the new year because of a shin injury but Carrick was boosted by Kobbie Mainoo’s return to training this week.

title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Sugar’
author: Antonio Losada
text:
All of a sudden, the Knicks look scary.

Who would have thought after they won the championship four months ago lost three in a row!?

Here’s the latest as the guys rest up for their NBA Cup title-defending debut on Friday.

On why Mo Diawara and Pacome Dadiet haven’t played this season:

“It’s tough because going into the season early on, one of [the] things I wanted to experiment with is playing 10 or 10 ½ guys [as my rotation]. And Mo is in that mix. Mo and Pac. Give them different opportunities at different times. And we experimented with different stuff and our players not getting it done caused us to start off a little slow.

“So to get us on track, we’re going to hold the fort down with a veteran group of guys. Hopefully we get to the point sooner than later that I can start throwing those [young] guys out there.”

On continuing to experiment with the Knicks’ bench rotation:

“Our starting five is what it is. But everybody else after that, until we find something that’s working consistently, I’m going to try to give different guys opportunities.”

On Jalen Brunson overcoming his shooting struggles against Chicago:

“I wasn’t worried about that. He just seems like he always finds a way. And tonight we needed every single one of those. It definitely wasn’t a concern of mine.”

On the Knicks looking sluggish after arriving in Chicago at 2:30 a.m.:

“It was just a late game [Tuesday night]. I acknowledged that to our guys. It’s not an excuse. It’s the life of the NBA. So we have to find a way in situations like this, and our guys found a way. But you could tell we looked really, really sluggish.”

On Brunson’s determination, toughness and MVP-caliber ability:

“His will is unbelievable. His determination, man, it’s second to none. You look at this guy and he’s not 6-7, he’s not athletic, he’s not quick. I mean, you can go down the line in natural physical tools that a lot of guys have, but his determination, his spirit, his competitive spirit, his will, his toughness, especially his mental toughness, but his physical toughness, too, added with his skill set, it makes him an unbelievable basketball player. An MVP-caliber basketball player. I hope he gets recognition for that this year because his will is off the charts.”

On benching Mikal Bridges and using Tyler Kolek alongside Brunson on Wednesday:

“We just found a combination we went with. One of the things [assistant coach] Rick Brunson suggested was throwing Kolek in the game with Jalen. Just to give them a different look and get Jalen off the ball and put Tyler on the floor.

“Doing that, playing Jordan Clarkson extended minutes, Landry was playing well. Now there’s not much room. And the combination we had out there, we kept playing well. It was harder to go back to what we started with.”

On Karl-Anthony Towns continuing to shoot after injuring his left hand and wrist:

“He was still shooting that thang from 30 feet. So the wrist looked good to me.”

On whether the Knicks are generating good shots despite their early shooting struggles:

“The biggest thing is: are we getting good shots from the right people? Watching the film and watching the game, I think we are. We’ve had some pretty good looks from the right people at the right time that normally go in so I want them to keep shooting.”

On what Tyler Kolek needs to improve as the Knicks’ backup point guard:

“He’s gotta run the team. What I mean by that is, when you watch our games, when he goes on the floor, people get up into his chest when he’s trying to run our offense. He can’t get off the ball too early, if it’s just one guy. He’s gotta be able to go by that guy and get the guy off-balance and bring it back out and set our offense up and/or get by and make a play in the paint. He can’t let pressure bother him or disrupt our offense at all.

“And then defensively, he’s gotta be a pest. He’s gotta be nasty, not anything illegal or anything like that, just a guy that people wanna say ‘get off me, get off me,’ because he’s more than capable of doing that. He’s gotta play with some sort of force, particularly for his size.”

On the Knicks’ bench contributions in their comeback victory over Chicago:

“We got a lot of contributions from all across the board. I thought our bench was fantastic. Landry came off the bench and had 14 points, 4-for-7 from the three-point line was huge. Andre Drummond came off the bench and had 11 rebounds in 15 minutes. That was huge. Tyler hit three big threes, nine assists in 18 minutes. Zero turnovers; he’s just a ball mover. That was huge.

“And obviously our defensive player of the game, Jordan Clarkson. He was big for us. He had been on the shelf for a while. Not only was he big for us offensively, but he had two big steals for us during our run. Our bench was very good for us tonight.”

On overcoming his shooting slump and rediscovering his rhythm against the Bulls:

“I was happy to be able to kind of finally get over that hump. I feel like I was putting a lot of unnecessary commentary in my head. But seeing the ball go in the way it did, it put me out of my mental state and put me in a good flow state.”

On how he broke out of the slump:

“I switched a couple of things up.”

On his relationship with Derrick Rose and Rose’s son, P.J.:

“It’s crazy to see how old he is now. I’m thankful for the relationship I have with him and his family. I feel like the feeling is mutual. I’m happy to have (Derrick) as a mentor and someone I can talk to, and someone I look up to, as well.”

On his memories of growing up around Chicago basketball and attending Bulls games:

“So many memories. I remember the Eastern Conference finals with Derrick, when they lost to LeBron, and going to all of those games. I met Kobe here. I met countless players here. Just how loud the United Center was — it’s always going to be loud no matter the situation. So many memories. I remember exactly where I used to sit and everything. It was perfect.”

On Jalen Brunson, Karl-Anthony Towns and OG Anunoby after facing the Knicks:

“Jalen Brunson cold. Then KAT is just––he’s huge, he’s huge, he just makes the right decision, can shoot, trail threes, just plays the basketball really well. Honestly, they’re just a good team. OG’s really good too, really physical, hard to go against, hard to score against, they just have a really well-rounded team.”

title: 'Fully committed' Fernandes to remain Man Utd captain
text:
Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick says Bruno Fernandes is "fully committed" to the club and will continue as captain.

Carrick dropped Fernandes to the bench for Sunday's 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after the Portuguese questioned the tactics used in a 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como.

The defeat by Bournemouth left Carrick's future hanging by a thread, but the 45-year-old will be in charge for Saturday's trip to Chelsea.

It remains to be seen whether Fernandes will return to the starting line-up, but the pair held clear-the-air talks at United's Carrington training ground on Tuesday in a bid to move forward.

Carrick says there is "no decision to be made" over whether Fernandes remains captain.

"We are clear with the situation of the team, and as a football club," said Carrick.

"He [Fernandes] is an important player for this group. He has been and he will be.

"We've got to make a difference and we've got to push things in a good direction.

"He's fully committed to this football club; he's fully committed to making things better. There are absolutely no issues with that.

"It doesn't change for me. It was a decision for what we felt for the [Bournemouth] game. That's it.

"He's the one that's led the team so well for many a game and many a year, and he'll continue to do that. There are absolutely no issues with that."

Carrick and Fernandes hold clear-the-air talks

United have gone eight games without a win as they head to Chelsea - their worst run of results since 2015-16.

Not since the 1988-89 campaign have they had a sequence of nine matches without a win.

Nearly 40 hours passed between United losing against Bournemouth on Sunday and the club providing clarification on Carrick's future, with the Englishman being given a chance to turn things around at Old Trafford.

Talks involving the Glazer family, minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox took place before Carrick's immediate future was confirmed.

It seems likely he will remain in post for next Tuesday's Champions League match against Roma, and the Premier League encounter with Aston Villa at Old Trafford on 8 November, after which there is a two-week international break.

Carrick, though, says he does not need guarantees over his position.

"I don't need any assurances from anyone," he said.

"I totally get the position. I understand the job. I understand the responsibilities. I understand what comes with that. So, I really don't need any assurances from anyone in that regard."

Asked if he was surprised to still be in a job, Carrick said: "No. I'm here to do my job. I'm here to do the best for the team, and I'm desperate to make us better and improve things. So, I'm not surprised, no."

title: How £100 vanishes in minutes: inside the ‘slot farms’ targeted in the budget
author: Rob Davies
text:
John Healey has hit adult gaming centres with 25% tax. Undercover footage shows how they lure customers

The last of five £20 notes disappears into the slot machine as The Verve’s Bittersweet Symphony plays over the shop’s sound system.

That’s it, £100 gone in the space of about five minutes, swallowed up by one of the many “slot farms” that dominate the shopping streets of Peterborough .

All that’s left to show for it is a free KitKat, one of the incentives staff use to tempt customers into staying a little longer and losing a little more.

It’s lunchtime on a Thursday and dozens of glassy-eyed hopefuls are having the same experience, feeding in what little cash they have and cursing as it disappears.

The same pattern is repeated across the country. Gamblers in Great Britain lost £2.7bn on slot machines last year, nearly double the annual budget of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, which oversees the sector.

In his inaugural budget this week, the chancellor, John Healey, took direct aim at slot machines by raising “machine games duty”, the tax levied on them, from 20% to 25%. This, he said, would bring in nearly £150m a year, “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.

But what is the reality of Britain’s booming slot machine industry and why is it in the government’s crosshairs?

That’s one reason why each machine earns £40,000 a year on average, more than the median pay of a British worker. Slot machines are found in bookmakers, casinos and bingo halls but the venues that really pack them are adult gaming centres (AGCs), sometimes known as slot farms.

They’re on pretty much every British high street, disproportionately in poorer areas . On some, such as this stretch in Peterborough, almost every shop is a bookmaker or an AGC.

By far the two biggest AGC operators are Admiral, which is owned by an Austrian billionaire, and Merkur, owned by a German billionaire. Both have targeted the UK for growth in recent years.

AGCs have their critics, including Andy Burnham, who has accused them of “ targeting some of the most vulnerable in our communities”. Notable examples include when Merkur was fined £100,000 in 2025, after the Guardian revealed it had allowed an older woman with terminal cancer to rack up huge losses over two spells lasting 16 hours.

As well as the potential for rapid losses, the machines are associated with higher rates of problem gambling than products such as sports betting. Critics also point to practices apparently designed to keep punters playing and losing. For a start, the majority of venues are open 24 hours a day , while the Guardian has previously revealed that staff are paid bonuses linked to customers’ losses , undermining their incentive to intervene to prevent problem gambling.

Shops are increasingly offering a new breed of super slot machine, featuring a comfy armchair and a highly-immersive, 65-inch screen. Staff will offer drinks and snacks to keep punters playing, there are regular prize draws and “free spin” offers, and you can make cash withdrawals from your bank without leaving the shop.

Punters will sometimes play more than one machine simultaneously. Admiral has introduced a two-machine limit, which it says is designed to reduce harmful gambling.

Many are open under bingo licences, which may sound more benign to local authority planning committees. In practice, most have one bingo machine that is rarely used, if ever.

On a one-off basis, it’s possible to win up to £500. In tests across several AGC venues, the Guardian occasionally won some money, which will be donated to charity. But the machines have a fixed “return to player”, meaning that regular slot machine players will always lose. That’s why slots are a good target for a tax raid, and a valuable cash cow for companies, which like predictable sources of income. It’s also why gambling harm experts think they’re dangerous.

Bookmakers say it will cost them money, leading to shop closures. Entain, which owns Ladbrokes, expects a £25m hit. But shares in the three listed slot machine operators – Entain, the William Hill owner Evoke and the Grosvenor Casinos owner Rank Group – rose sharply after the budget. Relieved investors had feared Healey would opt for a 40% rate.

AGCs were singled out by the chancellor, who said they and vape shops would be excluded from business rates relief, costing them a combined £10m. But AGCs appear well-placed to thrive anyway because of their low overheads and 24-hour opening. For the slot farms, it’s business as usual.

Neither Admiral nor Merkur responded to a request for comment. Bacta, the slot machine trade body, said its members’ venues were “among the safest places to gamble, with experienced staff on hand to identify problems and provide support to customers”.

“Player protection is central to our approach, and machines in AGCs are designed with inbuilt tools to encourage safe play, facilitate self-exclusion and help prevent problem gambling,” it said.

“Games in these venues are low-stake – costing as little as 10p a spin – and these businesses have been a longstanding part of the high street for decades, providing low-stake entertainment, local jobs and a boost to local economies. AGCs tend to open on high streets where there is already footfall, alongside other hospitality and leisure venues, and where planning and licensing permissions allow.

“Our members operate within one of the most tightly regulated licensing regimes in the world. Venues are regularly inspected, must comply with strict conditions, and can have licences refused or revoked where licensing objectives are at risk.”

title: Zwift Plus Review: The Premium Tier That Could Replace Strava
author: Josh Ross
text:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Video routes mean more routes Lots of new badges to chase Quality machine learning based structured training system Workouts use group rides and RoboPacers instead of just ERG mode Immediate post-ride coach analysis on pacing and fatigue

Requires an upgraded Zwift Plus premium subscription When deviating from the plan feedback is unclear

Today, Zwift is launching Zwift Plus. This new premium tier pushes the monthly cost to $29.99, with a discounted yearly option at $299.99. In exchange for the upcharge, you unlock two core upgrades: real-world video routes and adaptive coaching.

Zwift considers this a massive milestone, which is why I recently went to Moab to celebrate the video-based routes ahead of launch. The concept was to ride the route indoors, then ride it outdoors to see how perfectly they matched. Unfortunately, we caught the tail end of a Pacific hurricane, so I only got to drive the route and ride it inside. Still, the big reveal ended up feeling almost anti-climactic—but in the best way possible.

The inside perfectly matches the real world, but you still get all the Zwift details you are used to. Zwift lays the graphics seamlessly into high-resolution and high frame rate footage. I rode the Tron bike in Arches National Park, and while it sadly doesn’t glow on the road, the wheels sit perfectly on the video road and the speed adjusts as you ride without ever breaking the illusion. It’s underwhelming, but only because it’s really good and feels like a natural extension of what Zwift already does. If you’ve used Rouvy, which Zwift now owns, this is better.

Personally, though, I don’t find the video-based routes all that much of a draw. They provide more variety, and that’s great, but Zwift already adds routes all the time and anyone who’s used Zwift knows the team is great at recreating real-life locations. What this launch is really all about is coaching, and that’s where the real magic is.

Part of why the team at Zwift considered this launch such a high-stakes proposition is that it’s a price increase, and that always comes with baggage. You could even consider the addition of the video routes to the Zwift Plus plan as a sort of tiered pricing structure where, all of a sudden, you have to pay for more routes. That’s not really true, but I can understand the hesitation.

I think part of why I don’t see that as an issue is because I don’t find the video routes to be the major news here. They are additional content, and as someone who will likely chew through every single additional badge Zwift offers this winter, that’s nice, but also not a big deal. Instead, I see this as a pretty clear value proposition of $10 a month for structured training.

With that in mind, my favorite thing about Zwift Plus is that I see it as a product that is going to consolidate the structured training market. I believe this will be a big hit to TrainerRoad, and I think that for many people, Zwift Plus will represent a net decrease in monthly subscriptions.

The reasons for this are pretty simple: structured training has to be good enough, and it has to create an environment where the user actually follows the plan. Before this launch, Zwift was mostly failing at both of those requirements.

Zwift already had training plans; they just weren’t engaging, they weren’t reactive, and they were widely considered to be not that great. With Zwift Plus, the first correction was the quality of the plans, and to address that, Zwift brought on Ryan Cooper.

If you aren’t familiar with the name, Ryan Cooper is the founder of Best Bike Split and the former Chief Scientist at TrainingPeaks. To understand why his involvement is so important, you have to look at what Best Bike Split actually does. It is a predictive physics engine that takes a rider’s specific power profile, weight, and aerodynamics, layers it over the exact elevation of a race course, and calculates exactly how many watts that rider should push on every single segment to finish as fast as possible without blowing up.

That is the level of data-driven modeling he brings to Zwift, and it is exactly why the brand is very careful to call this new coaching system “machine learning” rather than “AI.” Right now, AI is a marketing buzzword. When most people hear it, they picture a chatbot scraping the internet and hallucinating a generic training plan based on a text prompt.

Machine learning is different. It relies on math and datasets. In this case, Cooper’s algorithms were trained on the anonymized power and heart rate data of millions of Zwift riders, combined with peer-reviewed sports science. The system isn’t guessing or estimating based on what it read online. It uses actual machine learning to recognize patterns in your specific history, power data, and daily fatigue, and then mathematically calculates exactly what you need to do today to actually get faster.

This means Zwift has now solved the quality problem that TrainerRoad has so far always held as an advantage. But the raw quality of workouts is actually somewhat secondary in real life. You need not only quality workouts, but you need workouts that people will complete, and this is where Zwift has something no one else does.

Zwift controls everything about where you ride your bike, and that means the Zwift Plus workout plan has options. Once you set up your plan, the system will recommend an ever-changing variety in terms of how you complete a workout. My favorite example was actually the first day of the 12-week plan I started, when I was scheduled for a route rather than a set of intervals.…

title: Zwift reveals higher subscription tier with AI coach, adaptive training plans and real-world video
author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
text:
As indoor trainer season starts gathering momentum faster than an avatar down a virtual mountain, product updates and new launches are coming thick and fast.

MyWhoosh came with zombie chases, Tacx dropped the Nera smart trainer, and Zwift teased a few more Californian routes, but today’s announcement is one that’s sure to shake things up good and proper.

It comes in the form of Zwift Plus, a new higher-priced premium subscription tier that, certainly at first glance, appears to borrow features from a number of its competitors, no doubt closing the feature gap in a bid to capture a greater share of the market.

The first part is the integration of adaptive training and an artificial intelligence ‘Zwift Coach’ that can help you set a goal, analyse workouts, and adapt as time passes in line with progress.

The second part is the unveiling of new real-world video-based routes, as opposed to the virtual worlds – or digital recreations thereof – which Zwift has committed to and relied upon thus far.

Adaptive training and Zwift Coach

AI is the buzzword of the year, and it’s no surprise to see Zwift, whose headquarters lie just a stone's throw from Silicon Valley, lean into the technology.

Zwift says there’s a strong correlation between consistency and fitness gains, including three main claims:

Those who ride twice a week are 2.8x fitter than those who ride once every two weeks

Those with a 12-week streak see an increase of up to 12% in their FTP.

Riders on a training plan see their FTP grow by 4.15%, versus 1.97% for those without one.

The Zwift Coach, therefore, aims to get more of those people onto a plan and riding consistently, setting a plan that aligns with goals set from the outset, and then “adapts to life” in real time, as sessions are completed, failed, or skipped.

The integration of video is the second major upgrade exclusive to Plus subscribers, and despite some of Zwift’s competitors – and indeed its new subsidiary, Rouvy – offering footage filmed by users, Zwift will use footage obtained exclusively by an in-house team of videographers.

The feature will launch with 21 routes across the following destinations:

The French Alps: Col du Galibier, Cime de la Bonnette

Mallorca: Sa Calobra, Coll de Femenia

Western Cape: Chapman's Peak, Bains Kloof

Lofoten Islands: The Midnight Sun Road

Southern Utah: The Hogsback, Arches NP

The Scottish Highlands: Glen Etive

The routes will include digitally created finish line banners and blimps in the sky, bringing a touch of the familiar Zwift gameplay to users, but will ultimately bring more destinations to the Zwift world.

The new subscription tier will be priced at a £9 / €10 / $10 / AU$15 upcharge over the current price, meaning a monthly subscription will be £26.99 / €29.99 / $29.99 / AU$44.99.

Annual subscriptions allow users to get 12 months for (almost) the price of 10. These are charged at £269.99 / $299.99 / €299.99 / $449.99.

The existing Zwift tier is still available, and the prices for that remain unchanged.

'Painful' years ahead, think tanks warn, as living standards set to fall
text:
People are facing a "painful" and "depressing" few years ahead, economic think tanks have warned, after forecasts showed growth in living standards grinding almost to a halt.

Typical working-age households would see their disposable income fall by £1,050, or 3%, between now and 2029, according to the Resolution Foundation, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the current decade would be the worst for household income growth on record.

Chancellor John Healey said his Budget offered "breathing space", but said the government could "never remove completely" cost of living pressures.

The UK's official forecaster said its latest economic forecast painted a "pretty grim picture".

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), blamed the difficult financial situation facing the UK on higher borrowing costs and inflation caused by the US-Iran war.

In response to rising energy prices, Healey has announced measures, including a £100 support payment, aimed at easing pressure on household finances.

But that would not be enough to offset the impact of higher energy bills, the Resolution Foundation said.

"This parliament is increasingly looking like one of two halves," said the think tank's chief executive, Ruth Curtice.

"The first half has been marked by rising living standards, solid economic growth and extra funding for public services," she said.

However, the second half of the parliament would be "tough going", she said.

Treasury will not commit to reducing welfare bill before next election

What we now know about the UK economy in four charts

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you

In response the government had provided a "scattergun" Budget that did not do enough to address the challenges facing the country, Curtice said.

Over the course of this parliament, incomes for non-pensioner households, after taxes, benefits, and housing costs are taken into account, will have risen by "a paltry" £600, the Resolution Foundation said, with the gains made in the first five years.

Even after the extra support provided by the government, households will be left paying higher energy bills than during the last energy crisis in 2022, according to its analysis.

The Resolution Foundation said the support should have been more targeted at the poorest households.

Alongside the Budget the OBR issued its economic forecast indicating a slowdown in GDP growth from 1.2% in 2026 to 1% in 2027.

The forecast for next year is sharply lower than what was predicted at their last assessment in March.

The OBR also put its forecast for inflation for 2027 up from 2% to 3.4%.

Frozen tax thresholds are also eating into people's take-home pay.

However, the OBR also emphasised the difficulties in economic forecasting, highlighting uncertainty over the future path of inflation, in particular, which could turn out to be either significantly higher or lower than their predictions.

While the Resolution Foundation focused its forecast for living standards on working age households, the OBR looks at all households, including pensioners and reflects a 10-year rolling average growth to take into account short-term fluctuations.

The OBR found that by the end of the decade living standards for all households would have barely grown, by less than 0.1% per year.

"This decade looks set to be the worst decade for growth in household incomes on record," added the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS).

"No amount of temporary cost of living packages will fix that. We need a stronger economy."

IFS director Helen Miller said there would also be growing pressure on the government's spending plans over the parliament.

"Spending plans look extremely tight. They don't look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver," she said.

"Whether or not they are delivered matters because the spending plans underpin the plan to bring down borrowing," she added.

Miller said she was left with the impression that Healey was hoping the economy would improve to take the pressure off those spending decisions.

Healey, speaking on the BBC's Today Programme, said "economic storms", including the Iran war and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, were affecting countries around the world and the government was seeking to help where it could.

He said energy bill help would create "breathing space" for most households.

Around 20 million households are set to receive the £100 payment based on which council tax band they are in.

But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the Budget had left the public finances "more fragile" as Healey had reduced the "headroom" of the amount of buffer the country has between what it takes in revenues and what it spends.

Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said the £100 energy payment would be identified as the best item in the Budget for many people, but said that it was "not good enough" when you considered the "stealth tax rises" that were taking money out of people's pay packets.

title: 'This shouldn't happen' – Paul Seixas joins calls for greater rider safety following death of Finlay Tarling
author: James Moultrie
text:
Paul Seixas has continued the call for better safety in the peloton following the death of British rider Finlay Tarlin g at the Volta a Portugal in August, who was killed after colliding with a non-race vehicle that had entered the course.

These included Coppa Bernocchi – where a DHL delivery van driver turned onto the course – and Tre Valli Varesine – where a police motorbike hit two Pinarello Q36.5 riders – two of the Italian Autumn Classics that serve as the build-up to Il Lombardia, where Seixas made history as the youngest-ever winner .

The young French superstar got emotional as he emphasised the need for better safety standards once more, having raced against Tarling several times, including at the junior World Championships and junior Liège-Bastogne-Liège as they both developed towards professional careers.

"Honestly, it's terrible. The problem is, he's not the only one," said Seixas.

"What's more, I raced with him, and it really affects me. It really affected me at the time, because what's terrible is that we'll be thinking: 'This is yet another cyclist who has died in a race this year.'"

The protest at Il Lombardia came about through a WhatsApp group with Tom Pidcock and Ben Healy spearheading the idea, which was kept quiet from teams and the CPA – the rider union – and coincided with a statement being released en masse by riders on social media.

Seixas didn't mince his words as he detailed how serious the call is for greater safety, admitting just how scary bike racing can be when incidents like what happened in Portugal are still possible.

"I think it really affected everyone, all the riders. That's when you realise that sometimes there are real organisational problems; the organisers do their best, that's not what we're saying, but sometimes there should be more strict standards," he said.

"We protested about it at Lombardia, at the beginning of the race, for five minutes. What happened is extremely serious. Families are affected. It's very serious that it happened during a race. A professional organisation, riders losing their lives; it's frightening."

Seixas talked about how while he hasn't had a major crash himself, the risks of racing can enter a rider's mind at the most dangerous parts of a race, and while noting that accidents and crashes are unfortunately part and parcel of professional bike racing, a death like Tarling's simply should not happen.

"Let's just say that sometimes you get a little stressed, but you don't think it's for your life either. When you're in a peloton, there's a false flat downhill, and you're going 80 kph, sometimes you're still a little scared," said the Frenchman.

"You think to yourself: 'Now, it could be… Serious', but you must not think about it; that's the thing. And you know that everyone else is aware of it too, so they're not going to do anything reckless either. Then, sometimes there's nervousness; that's what can make everyone tense and create danger.

"When there are falls, yes, you get injured, but on the road, I've never had a fracture or a sprain; I've never had anything. Scratches, that's happened to me, several times, many times even. But you always come out of it well. Afterwards, there have been very serious falls in history, but riders who find their death like that in a race, that shouldn't happen."

title: 'You try to survive' – Esmée Peperkamp adds her name to the criticism of the culture at Picnic-PostNL
author: Owen Rogers
text:
After spending five seasons with Picnic-PostNL, Esmée Peperkamp has added her voice to those criticising the management and support structures at the Dutch team.

In an interview with Dutch broadcaster , Peperkamp said her health and form deteriorated during her time with Picnic, described the medical support at Picnic as "substandard" and alleged she was told to train through injury.

She also stated that all the riders and staff she worked with have contractual clauses preventing them from publicly criticising the team, even after they have left.

Peperkamp alleged the team is guilty of negligence, saying: "You are never listened to and that things are decided for you that are ultimately not good for you."

Now in the middle of a two-year deal at VolkerWessels, Peperkamp arrived at what was then Team DSM in 2021, aged 23, as a promising climber. She left at the end of the 2025 season with only six top-10 placings to her name.

Peperkamp was one of several riders NOS spoke to anonymously in their original story about the culture of the team, but she has now decided to go public, so she can both help others and explain her continuing poor health.

"My health is still deteriorating because I still do not produce enough hormones," she told . "I haven't had a period since 2021, and I have RED-S, relative energy deficiency in sport. I contracted that during my time at DSM and later at Picnic-PostNL."

"Whether you got your period, for example, was never a question. It was never checked whether my hormone levels were in order, even though there are annual health checks. This could have been prevented."

After suffering a concussion at the 2024 Vuelta a Burgos, she alleged she was left unsupported, adding: "They handled it very casually. For example, they left it up to me whether I would train the next day."

Peperkamp also explains that she suffered from irritable bowel syndrome and a lactose intolerance, which meant she struggled with the nutrition provided by the team, though she was not allowed a substitute.

"I became very sick. So nauseous that I couldn't eat anymore. I was vomiting too. I could feel sick for days and therefore ate very little. I just had to get used to it, they said. I sometimes had kind caregivers who gave me bottles with regular isotonic drink, or water.

"You try to survive, to get yourself noticed by other teams, to keep your dream alive."

Having moved to VolkerWessels this season, Peperkamp has not raced since failing to finish Liège-Bastogne-Liège in April.

While Peperkamp is one of several former riders to have criticised the team, others have come out in support, with John Degenkolb questioning why voices like his were not included in ’s reporting.

In response, the team have appointed lawyer Professor Marjan Olfers to lead an independent enquiry into the team’s culture. Olfers has a long history working in professional sport, leading the investigation surrounding Michael Rasmussen’s presence at and exclusion from the 2007 Tour de France

Picnic-PostNL issued the following statement to : "We regret that a member of our team experienced matters such as those you describe. As previously announced, we will have an independent investigation conducted into this matter.

"For various reasons, we cannot comment on individual cases as outlined by the NOS. Firstly, it concerns an anonymous complaint, making it difficult for us to respond specifically.

"In addition, we do not share information about individual team members with third parties, even when we suspect who is involved. This policy is partly aimed at safeguarding the privacy of the (former) riders mentioned by you, as well as the privacy of the many team members, on and off the bike, who work or have worked together (intensively), and thus to prevent them from feeling unsafe due to the sharing of such information."

title: Thibau Nys to kick off cyclo-cross campaign at Koppenbergcross after challenging road season
author: Matilda Price
text:
The Koppenbergcross has been run 36 times, and almost a third of those editions have been won by a member of the Nys family, with Sven winning nine times in the 2000s before his son Thibau Nys took up the mantle in 2023 and 2025.

Nys junior will be hoping to make it 12 wins for the Belgian cyclo-cross dynasty this weekend as he kicks off his campaign at Koppenbergcross – officially the Oudenaarde round of the X2O Badkamers Trofee – on Sunday.

Given he has already won this iconic event, with takes in the famous cobbled Koppenberg climb in Flanders, Nys is targeting nothing less than victory in his first race back on the mud this season.

"Otherwise, I cannot be satisfied," he told as he trained on the course on Wednesday, with his father and a smattering of fans in attendance.

"I am very well aware that it will not be easy, perhaps the most difficult edition of the last few years for me. But on the Koppenberg, I cannot be happy with a podium finish."

The main reason Nys expects a tougher edition than usual is that he's had a particularly short preparation period for his cyclo-cross season. That's because he raced the Vuelta a España in September and then the Road World Championships, giving him only a few weeks to switch to CX training.

"Because everything had to be crammed into three weeks, I was unable to do quite a few important training sessions," he said. "And those are precisely the sessions that can provide a confidence boost. So we’ll have to make do with it and hope it’s enough."

Starting with possibly the most important race for him personally seems like both throwing himself back in at the deep end and a way to ensure he hits the ground running, with chasing his father's record of nine wins something of a career goal for the 23-year-old.

"I want to win that race as many times as possible in my career, more than, for example, wanting to become European Champion," he said, though he has won the stars-and-stripes jersey before, and will be in the team in the Netherlands in mid-November.

"That doesn't mean I prefer the Koppenberg over Zeddam [host of the European Championships] in two weeks right now, but after my career, I would rather be able to say that I managed to win on the Koppenberg seven or eight times than that I became European Champion seven times."

There is also perhaps extra pressure on Nys to put together a successful 'cross campaign this winter given how tough his road season was. He underwent knee surgery in March, which required a long period away from racing – he missed the first six months of the year – meaning he could only fit in 30 race days and had no wins.

He took third on a stage of the Vuelta, but was then a DNF at the Road Worlds. But with his knee seemingly in full working order again, he can hope to stand on the top step of a podium again soon – as soon as this weekend, he hopes.
