title: I earn £30,000. I'm angry there was no fuel duty cut in the Budget
text:
Chancellor John Healey has unveiled his first Budget.

He announced £100 energy payment for millions and a tax rise on banks, among other measures.

BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and how the Budget affects them.

Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.

He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.

He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."

The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump.

The only measure Dave wanted to see was a cut to fuel duty, and he was disappointed this didn't happen.

"I'm pretty angry, really. Nothing has been thrown my way," he says.

The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, and it will be frozen again, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."

Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college.

The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers.

"I'm trying my best, it's all you really can do. It's kind of suffocating in a way. You see everyone else managing, and you feel like you're not."

Emily was initially disappointed with the Budget, and then frustrated that the government is waiting for the outcome of a review into youth unemployment before legislating next year.

"I'm glad the government is aware, and that they have a plan," she said. "But it's a bit frustrating that we have to wait a little longer to find out what it is."

However, she adds: "It's not happened today, but it will happen."

She wants to see more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government's Jobs Guarantee , external scheme extended.

The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.

Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.

Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.

"Council tax and energy bills would add to it. Food too. I'd need a TV licence, broadband, my car and some money to socialise. By that point I'd be in the minus."

Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax.

The Budget "doesn't go far enough", he says, adding he would have liked to have seen more help with the cost of living, including a cut in fuel duty.

The £100 household energy allowance over a year is less than £10 a month, he says, while action on tariffs on food items will save only £21 a year, or £1.75 per month.

"What am I going to buy with that - a Freddo?"

He would like to get on the housing ladder but for now it feels a distant prospect. The government has announced a scheme to help first-time buyers in England who have a deposit of 2.5%, but Robert says: "Saving for a house is impossible at the moment."

Chloe Chin-Saad's husband passed away four years ago and her biggest worry is the cost of living.

She's very grateful that the rent she pays on her south London maisonette is set below the market rate as it is housing association accommodation, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."

She lives with her 16-year-old son, and says her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity.

"We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."

Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.

But she can't do anything to reduce her £200 council tax bill, the £250 a month she pays on car finance, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.

Two mobile phone bills, and food and pet insurance for her dog also add to her costs. She says the amount she has left over at the end of each month varies, and sometimes she is left with as little as £50.

Chloe says she is "pretty happy" with the Budget, and that "small changes give me hope".

Cutting standing charges on gas, and the £100 household energy payment for households in council tax bands A to D this winter are "definitely going to help", she says.

"It was quite a thoughtful Budget," she adds. "I can see, in years to come, light at the end of the tunnel."

Jonathan Whitwam, who recently joined the Labour Party, works in finance and says, in addition to his mortgage, his biggest outgoing is supporting his two daughters through university. He and his wife, who live in Essex, pay their rent, which is around £18,000 per year.

His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year.…

title: Sometimes managers need sacking for own good - Neville
text:
Gary Neville says managers sometimes need to be sacked "for their own good" as he reflected on Manchester United 's decision to persist with under-pressure Michael Carrick.

United are 16th in the Premier League, just one point above the relegation zone, following a dismal 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on Sunday.

Carrick was widely expected to be sacked after that loss, but the club have opted to give the 45-year-old head coach the opportunity to turn things around, and he will remain in charge for United's trip to Chelsea on Saturday lunchtime.

"I reckon what's happened in the 24 hours after Bournemouth is that they've literally debated it back and forth," former Manchester United captain Neville said on the Stick to Football podcast.

"I don't know this, but they've debated it to the point where they've got themselves into a muddle, and thought, 'we'll just stay with him'.

"I think staying with him is a result of the lack of planning, the lack of probably available options, the lack of decision-making around the two people that probably are available. That's when you're really struggling."

Neville added: "Sometimes a manager needs sacking for their own good. I needed sacking at Valencia. I was happy that they put me out of my misery."

Carrick's position was precarious even before the Bournemouth game after captain Bruno Fernandes criticised the tactics deployed in the 4-1 Champions League loss at Como last week.

Fernandes was dropped for the Bournemouth match, but he and Carrick have since held talks to clear the air.

"We've all been in football dressing rooms, and they're quite brutal places," Neville said.

"If Bruno Fernandes, the captain of the club... if he comes out and questions the manager's tactics after a 4-1 defeat in Como, where he's played like a drain, and he's been playing like a drain for three months, and the rest of them have as well, that is only 1 or 2% of what they're actually saying internally."

United fans sang Carrick's name as he applauded the crowd after the Bournemouth defeat during what Neville called "effectively a farewell lap".

Those fans then booed the players as soon as Carrick went down the tunnel.

It is understood United's hierarchy have explored the possibility of replacing Carrick, with ex- Newcastle United boss Eddie Howe and former Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann under consideration.

But, for now, the former Manchester United midfielder is left to bring the group together for Saturday's game at Stamford Bridge, with home fixtures against Roma and Aston Villa to follow before November's international break.

Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher said: "I think he can never say publicly, but I think Michael Carrick would want to be put out of his misery. I really do.

"The thought of going into that training ground now... and trying to do that team talk before Chelsea , when you know the players just aren't having it at all.

"Those players know Michael Carrick's not going to be there in two or three weeks. He knows it, they know it, everybody knows it."

Another former United captain, Roy Keane, added: "He needs the players more than they need him. That's football in a nutshell.

"The players know he's gone, but these are the same players who got him the job last year. So they're running the show."

title: The best indoor cycling accessories for under £50 / $50
author: Tim Perkin
text:
One of the big misconceptions regarding indoor cycling is that creating a suitable training space is expensive.

Purchasing a high-end smart trainer can be costly, but once you have it, the additional purchases that add the real value and make the biggest differences are surprisingly affordable.

Ultimately, a well-thought-out indoor setup is about more than just the bike and trainer. Comfort, cooling, and bike protection all help you train consistently and maximise every session.

Here are five useful, practical accessories priced under $50 that are worth investing in and will make your indoor cycling experience more enjoyable.

A bike mat is one of the first purchases to consider when setting up your indoor training space, particularly if you're mounting your outdoor bike on an indoor trainer.

The bike mat protects your carpet or flooring from grease, grime, or oil from your drive chain.

The bike mat also protects your flooring from sweat that accumulates during your sessions, as well as preventing deep indents in your carpet.

The mat can help contain sweat and make post-workout cleanup easier, and it's far less expensive to replace a mat than new carpet!

There is a range of mats on the market; it doesn't have to be a cycling-specific mat, and they can be found for under $50.

To protect your flooring, you may want to purchase some interlocking foam floor tiles. These are a popular option that can be laid on top of your carpet or garage flooring, creating a more level, stable base, depending on the flooring.

Effectively, it helps create a solid base on which to lay your bike mat and the best platform for your smart trainer and bike.

A pack of 12 can cost $49.99, with each tile measuring 24 in x 24 in, which totals 48 square feet.

A suitable fan is a must-have item for indoor cycling. Without the natural airflow you experience when riding outdoors, staying cool during indoor cycling can be a challenge, and things quickly get pretty uncomfortable.

A fan is essential for improving airflow, helping regulate your body temperature, and reducing the risk of overheating.

Choose a fan that suits your training space and budget. There is a range of fans available, but Amazon offers a basic fan for under $50 that would serve its purpose.

A small, foldable camping table is a useful item to purchase. This may seem slightly unconventional but is highly practical and very useful when undertaking long rides, races, or intense training sessions where you can place additional bottles and snacks within easy reach.

If you aren't within easy reach of a worktop or table, an extra table makes perfect sense; supplies can be lined up and kept close when needed. The small table also functions as a place to hold a secondary fan.

When you have finished your ride, simply wipe down the table and pack it away until your next longer session.

Prices vary, but there are plenty of options available for under $50.

Muc-Off offers an Indoor Training Kit, which normally retails for slightly over $50 but is currently on sale at $23.99 (usual price is slightly over $50, but such good value it’s worth including).

The Indoor Training Kit includes everything you need to keep yourself and your bike in top condition during indoor cycling sessions.

The kit features Antibacterial Equipment Cleaner to keep your training equipment fresh, Luxury Chamois Cream to help prevent chafing, and Sweat Protect to help protect your bike against sweat-related corrosion.

C3 Ceramic Dry Lube keeps your drivetrain running smoothly, while the Microfibre Cloth is ideal for cleaning and polishing your bike.

To complete the kit, a Muc-Off Tote Bag provides a convenient way to store and carry all your essentials.

Building a great indoor cycling setup doesn't have to cost a fortune. A few carefully chosen accessories can make your training sessions more comfortable, protect your flooring, and help keep your bike in good condition throughout the indoor season.

A bike mat and fan are excellent starting points, while protective floor tiles and a foldable table can make your training space more practical. Add a maintenance kit to the mix, and you'll be better equipped to handle everything from short weekday workouts to long indoor rides.

You don't need to buy everything at once. Start with the accessories that address your biggest needs, then upgrade your setup as your training demands grow. The goal is to spend wisely on products that make indoor cycling more enjoyable and hassle-free.

You Cannot Pogačar-Proof the Tour de France: Winners and Losers of the 2027 Route Reveal
author: Jim Cotton
text:
The Tour de France threw a curveball at the peloton last week when it revealed its route for 2027.

The most time trial kilometers in 15 years. The fewest summit finishes in recent memory. Too many very long stages.

The route for the 2027 Tour de France is about as old-school as you can get, and one that’s already been labeled anti-Pogačar, pro-Remco, and designed to delight great French hope Paul Seixas.

But is Pogačar’s chance at a historic sixth yellow jersey really in peril?

And can we on the couch really count ourselves lucky that the Montmartre finale returns to stage 21 in Paris? We’ve got to sit through one of the most featureless parcours of the Pogi era to see the Tour’s monumental modern ending.

Here are some of the biggest winners and losers from the 2027 Tour de France course reveal.

The 2027 Tour de France has been called the “anti-Pog” Tour de France .

But there’s no such thing. You cannot Pogačar-proof Le Tour.

The controversial inclusion of 71km of flat time trialing won’t have Tadej Pogačar in a fluster as he plans his shot at a record-breaking sixth maillot jaune.

At the 2026 Tour de France, time trial topper Remco Evenepoel finished more than six minutes back on Pogačar. Assuming they both hold form into next July, Evenepoel will need to gain five seconds per kilometer to level with King Pog.

If you think that’s going to happen, I want some of what you’ve been smoking.

Jonas Vingegaard and Visma-Lease a Bike’s Killer Bees were stung by the Tour route presentation. The 2027 parcours does not suit the two-time winner, not one bit.

With just three high-summit finishes, next year’s race looks more like an “anti-Jonas” Tour than an “anti-Pog” Tour.

The course includes only one of the high-altitude, multi-mountain monster stages where Vingegaard typically thrives. The 18th “Queen Stage” in the Pyrénées is the only obvious place where the Scandi climbing goat might drop his punchier rivals.

Vingegaard can’t rely on making much time in the Alps and Pyrénées, and he’s not likely to take time on the TT bike, either.

The 29-year-old’s three-year wait to reclaim the yellow jersey might see a new anniversary next year in Paris.

Everybody except a handful of heavy sprinters won when ASO confirmed the showstopper Montmartre would return to stage 21 of the Tour de France.

After two breathless thrillers won by Wout van Aert and Mathieu van der Poel – two of the biggest names in world cycling – in 2025 and 2026, nobody wanted to see a return of the fusty old bunch sprint format in 2027.

Go block it out of your calendar right now.

ASO didn’t let us have it all our own way by putting Montmartre back on the parcours for 2027.

Next year’s Tour de France is one of the longest of the past decade.

Three stages nudge past 220km, three are close to 200km, and only the finale in Paris clocks in at under 150km.

Strip the two time trials from the total distance of 3,479km, and the remaining road stages average 179km in length. That’s too long.

What happened to the trend toward always-entertaining, super-digestible three-hour stages? Bite-sized packages of 120-160km seemed like the future for a sport struggling to find a new audience.

The weekend stages 8, 15, and 20 – the days where the couch, your snack supply, and the Tour de France are the only things that matter – are all set up as sprints or breakaways.

Oh, and that nothing-burger 20th stage? Don’t get us started.

Remco Evenepoel isn’t any more likely to beat Tadej Pogačar at the 2027 Tour de France than he was in the 2026 Tour de France. He’d need an act of god or some mid-90s “preparation” to make that happen.

But Red Bull’s “aero bullet” is without doubt in pole position for second on the podium.

Evenepoel hasn’t seen a route this favorable in his entire career. In fact, he was some teenage football player the last time the Tour de France was so clearly designed for a time trialist. “The Wiggins Tour” included a mind-numbing 101km against the clock in 2012.

Evenepoel should gain more than enough advantage over 71km of time trialing to offset any potential losses in the mountains. He further benefits from the lack of multi-mountain stages and high summit finishes that have proven his kryptonite in the past.

There had been rumor that Evenepoel will target a Giro-Tour double in 2027.

There’s surely no way he’s considering messing around with such a risky schedule now.

The Tour de France promo spiel suggests there are seven sprint stages on tap for 2027, but the peloton’s reigning sprint king ain’t so sure.

Tim Merlier has grumbled that heavyweights like himself and Jonathan Milan might see as few as four chances next year. And given the return of the Montmartre, there’s not even the lure of the Champs-Élysées.

Indeed, the 2027 route is tilted in favor of “modern,” versatile sprinters like Matthew Brennan or Merlier’s rising teammate, Paul Magnier. Accumulated climbing or late obstacles could cook the carthorses before they see some of the “sprint finishes” promised them in next year’s Tour de France.

The only consolation for the biggest, “purest” sprinters?

A strong chance at winning the first yellow jersey at the stage 1 grand départ into Carlisle.

The French nation breathed a collective sigh of relief last week when Christian Prudhomme released the route for the 2027 Tour de France.

The kid’s a monster on the time trial bike, and he’ll have plenty of opportunity to reinforce that fact next July. He also seems better on smaller, punchier climbs than towering high Alps. How convenient then, that there are relatively few of those.

Tour organizers ASO have a habit of weighting the Tour’s parcours in favor of its rider du jour .

And while we’re not suggesting that’s the case in 2027 – how dare we?! – there’s nothing on the parcours that might stop Seixas from bettering his debut fourth-place finish from 2026 next July.

But is that really a good thing for the 20-year-old?…

title: 'I live with a ghost' - inside the haunted homes attracting bargain hunters
text:
From the moment Ryua first walked into her rental apartment in Tokyo she believed it to be haunted.

"When I visited the place for a viewing there was a man standing there, glaring at me," she says.

"Since the estate agent couldn't see him, I realised he must be a ghost."

While someone more squeamish would probably have quickly left the flat never to return, Ryua chose to go ahead and move in.

"I'm a bit of a contrarian, so I decided I wanted to become friends with this glaring male ghost," adds Ryua, who works as an aidoru, a young entertainer, and who doesn't wish to share her surname.

Four years later, and still in the same apartment, she says she continues to experience paranormal activity on a daily basis. She says she hears endless footsteps and the ghost talking.

Although Japan has increasingly marked Halloween , external in recent years, many Japanese people take ghosts seriously all year round. The country has a word, "yuurei", which means a lingering, troubled spirit.

These are the ghosts of people who died in violent or tragic circumstances - those who were murdered, killed themselves, or simply were lonely and died alone. If they died at home, then the belief is that their yuurei won't go away.

For house hunters who are not superstitious or squeamish it means there are big bargains to be found. There is a whole category of dwellings called jiko bukken, which means "stigmatised" or "incident" properties.

Under guidelines issued by the government in 2021, Japanese estate agents must disclose suicide, murder, death by fire, and any death where the body was not discovered for an extended period of time.

For rental properties this information must be disclosed for three years, and it must be revealed indefinitely for any property offered for sale.

By contrast, in the UK there is no legal requirement , external to reveal that a person died in a property. And in the US, it differs from state to state. , external For example, in California you have to reveal if a person has died in the property in the past three years, while in Arizona and Oregon you do not.

Ryua was told that a man had killed himself in her apartment. It meant that she gets an almost 30% discount on her rent on her tiny, 25 sq m bedsit in the fashionable ward of Setagaya. She says she pays 45,000 yen ($285; £213) a month, instead of what should have been 62,000 yen.

While a house where there had been a murder or suicide would probably be harder to sell or rent out anywhere in the world, Tokyo estate agent Erik Oskamp says that Japanese people are particularly superstitious and averse to stigmatised properties.

"[Even] an apartment next to a cemetery will be difficult to rent out, especially if you can see the tombs from the kitchen," explains Oskamp. "The worst thing is if a suicide has happened in the apartment. Even if somebody has jumped from the roof, many renters will move out. Other issues are a serious crime or a lonely death."

The latter issue, that of a person dying alone, would not generally affect the price of a property in, say, the UK or the US.

But in rural Kagoshima, in Japan's southwest, it enabled Diane Tincher to buy a large three-bedroom house for about half of what would have otherwise been the asking price.

The 79-year-old American has lived in Japan for nearly 40 years, working as a tour guide. She says that the estate agent had been straight with her – there was a heavy discount as an elderly lady had died alone, thereby stigmatising the property.

Tincher paid 20m yen for the house, in a location where similar properties usually sell for up to 45m yen.

"I don't believe in ghosts. But I know that the Japanese are very superstitious," she says. "If there is a ghost I'm thankful to her every day... to live in such a splendid and affordable home."

Researching the house, Tincher had found it on a website called Oshimaland, which lists jiko bukken properties, giving details of the events that occurred. It was launched in 2005 covering Tokyo, before expanding across Japan and then internationally in 2011.

It is crowdsourced, meaning that members of the public add the homes and their details.

Teru Oshima, the founder of Oshimaland, says that in the past such properties were "not very attractive options" in Japan.

Yet as house prices have surged in the country in recent years, as well as a big increase in the wider cost of living, one 2025 survey found that more than half of Japanese people would now rent a jiko bukken if it was cheap. , external

Back in Setagaya, Ryua says she is happy living with her ghostly flatmate. "I believe that ghosts were once living human beings, so they deserve our respect," she says.

title: Will Van der Poel and Van Aert race, Brand's dominance, and Van Empel's return – The storylines to follow this cyclo-cross season
author: Matilda Price
text:
The road season is over, the clocks have gone back, and the temperatures in Europe are dropping, which can mean only one thing: cyclo-cross is here.

The 2026-27 season is actually well underway by now, with the action kicking off in the US and Europe in September, but most of the main series are just starting or yet to begin.

The HG Cross series, formerly known as Exact Cross, is underway, while the Telenet Superprestige kicked off in Overijse at the weekend. The X2O Badkamers Trofee begins with its most iconic round, the Koppenbergcross, this weekend, whilst the headline series, the UCI Cyclo-Cross World Cup, will start on November 27 in Czechia.

The busy season, with series crowns up for grabs, plus national, Pan-American and European titles, builds towards the World Championships , which this season will be held in Oostende, Belgium at the end of January.

Whilst many of the races and protagonists stay the same year to year in 'cross, the plotlines and points of intrigue change and evolve each season, with different and exciting narratives running throughout the season, from the overall standings of each series to the competition building towards Worlds.

From the will-they-won't-they around Mathieu van der Poel and Wout van Aert to the exciting return of the prodigious Fem van Empel, there's plenty of interesting stories already brewing this winter – here's some you should be following this cyclo-cross season.

Definitely no big three, but what about the big two?

For the last decade, most of the intrigue around the men's calendar has revolved around the so-called 'big three': Mathieu van der Poel, Wout van Aert , and Tom Pidcock. They were cyclo-cross stars before they ever made it big on the road, and even as their WorldTour careers have grown, they've almost always made time during their winters to head back to the mud, with their first appearances circled in everyone's calendar.

This year, though, we won't get the big three – and we might not even get the big two.

That's because Tom Pidcock has already confirmed he won't be racing CX this season, and perhaps not in the future either, with road and mountain biking taking up more and more of his time, and the lack of an Olympic slot for CX, it's becoming harder for the Brit to justify adding the discipline to his schedule.

However, whilst we've been getting used to Pidcock doing less and less CX, what might be new this year is that we may not see Mathieu van der Poel in action, either. Wout van Aert has announced his intention to race at least some CX this year, though probably not starting until December, but the eight-time world champion might skip it altogether. He, too, has been doing less in recent years, but the imminent arrival of his first child seems to have only made his return to the fields even less likely.

So could we really be looking at our first CX season in years without the stars that have defined the last decade of the discipline? It certainly looks that way. In some ways, it might be good for the sport, as it opens up opportunities for the specialist to take more big wins, rather than being steamrolled by the blockbuster names when they turn up for a few races. But for the casual fans drawn in by Van der Poel and Van Aert, it might make for slightly less enthusiastic viewing.

Fem van Empel is back, and doing things differently

In women's CX, the biggest story of the season is undoubtedly Fem van Empel 's return to competition. Still only 24, Van Empel was a prodigious force in the discipline, winning practically at will for several seasons, but she stepped away last winter after repeatedly struggling with her mental health and motivation for racing.

No one knew then when she might return – if ever – but the Dutchwoman has found her groove earlier than expected, and is coming back to the sport this winter with Specialized TMRW , FDJ United-Suez's new off-road branch.

Formerly a prolific winner, it would be easy to expect Van Empel to return to those heights straight away. Instead, she and her team are doing things differently, making sure they don't repeat the mistakes of before, and that's really refreshing to see. For the moment, Van Empel is only racing a maximum of once per week, limiting the pressure on her and trying to enjoy being back first and foremost.

Of course, Van Empel's talent is such that even a gentle start has seen her already take fourth and fifth in her first races back, and it seems probable that she will return to winning ways this winter. But the important thing is that the pressure and tension is off, and Van Empel seems to have found the freedom to rediscover what she loves about racing. A winning Van Empel was good, but a happy one is even better.

Lucinda Brand just can't stop – but she will be challenged

Lucinda Brand has raced cyclo-cross since she was a teenager, and though she didn't start winning regularly at the top level until her sixth year as an elite, since then she's been a prolific victor and one of the most consistent riders on the circuit. So far this season, she's already won three of five races she's started, and she'll be chasing the whopping 20 victories she took last winter.

With the power of the rainbow bands, only the second time she's been world champion in her career, she's sure to be on another fantastic run, with zero signs of slowing down as she enters her final 18 months of professional racing.

However, if the races so far are anything to go by, it's not going to be a walk in the park for Brand, with other riders really stepping up to challenge her already. The returning Fem van Empel is an obvious candidate, but so are the likes of Blanka Vas and Shirin van Anrooij, who are changing teams this winter and returning to cyclo-cross with renewed motivation.

Among the specialists, Ceylin del Carmen Alvarado looked stronger than ever last winter and so far this year, while the likes of Denise Betsema and Aniek van Alphen haven't been much behind Brand either. Luxembourger Marie Schreiber seems to be finally finding a real groove, too, taking a big win at Nacht van Woerden, so the world champion certainly can't rest on her laurels.

Make way for the specialists

The upside to the absence of some of the big multidisciplinary stars this winter is that it will make room for more of the pure CX specialists to shine. These riders who commit their whole year to the discipline are sometimes outshone when the part-timers make their appearances, but with less of that on the cards this year, the series and big events should be contested more by the specialists.

On the men's side, Michael Vanthourenhout looks primed to step into the position of the season's dominant rider, and will perhaps be dreaming of a possible world title at the end of it, whilst riders like Cameron Mason look to be right on the verge of a first major level win. With younger riders like Niels Vandeputte and Witse Meussen on the up too, the men's series could be the most competitive we've seen in years, with plenty of chances of glory for the riders who make this discipline their bread and butter.

Who is going to have a breakout season?

And finally, on that topic, we'll be following closely to see who is going to make 2026-27 their breakout season, with plenty of talent rising to the top right now. There are a few names we have our eyes on already, but actually, the exciting thing is that there are a multitude of riders who could find that breakthrough result this year – the fun is in watching it happen, not trying to predict it in advance.

With the Belgian and Dutch riders naturally dominating the CX scene, even to this day, it's interesting to see who is coming up from outside the 'cross heartlands. US riders Mia Aseltine and Kaya Musgrave are both looking really strong on the European circuit, racing for Competitive Edge Racing, and Czech rider Kristýna Zemanová is on the cusp of a really big win – perhaps in one of the two World Cup rounds in her home country this November?

All series except the HG Cross have an overall series standing competition. The World Cup and Superprestige overalls are based on points, whilst the X2O Badkamers Trofee establishes its standings based on cumulative time across the series.

title: How will John Healey’s energy support package affect you?
author: Jillian Ambrose
text:
Chancellor’s ‘new course’ includes a £100 one-off payment, low-carbon upgrade loans and an end to standing charges

John Healey has unveiled a package of support for households being buffeted by “global economic storms”.

“I’m setting a new course to get energy costs down in line with Europe,” the chancellor said in his maiden budget. In the long term, he hopes that changes in how Britain covers the cost of renewables and grid upgrades will “drive down all aspects of energy bills”.

British households face some of the highest energy charges for three years, with the war in the Middle East driving up oil and gas prices.

Under the government’s price cap, average dual-fuel bills are £1,700 a year and could rise to more than £2,100 a year from January, according to industry forecasts .

So what has the chancellor offered hard-pressed households to help them through the coldest months of the year? And will it be enough to lower gas and electricity bills?

This measure will offer a modest saving for most British households – but not all, and perhaps not until next winter.

Healey promised to end “unfair and outdated” standing charges on gas bills for 23m homes “in 2027 or as soon as possible after”. This could help almost two-thirds of households to save an average of £45 a year.

A standing charge is a fixed daily fee paid through all household gas bills, regardless of how much is used. It means homes that severely ration their gas use – or use none at all – still shoulder the same cost as a high-income household.

The charge typically adds about £100 a year to bills and the change means these costs will soon be recovered through a higher unit price for gas. For those with below-average gas use, bills should fall. But there won’t be savings for everyone.

Jonny Marshall, an economist at the Resolution Foundation, said households with high gas use might have higher bills when the unit rate increases. These could include low-income households who have bigger families or poorly insulated homes.

A home using 7,000 kilowatt hours of gas a year would save about £40 under the change, but a household using 14,000 kWh of gas a year could be £25 worse off, according to Richard Neudegg, a director at Uswitch.com. A household using the typical 11,500 kWh shouldn’t see any change, he added.

The government has already begun taking aim at taxes and policy costs loaded on to electricity bills that could over time mean removing hundreds of pounds from bills.

This month, it removed the 5% VAT levy on electricity bills for 29m households, effectively saving them about £45 a year.

This was supposed to help households through the coldest months of the year, until March. But Healey has promised to keep VAT off bills until July, extending the annual savings to £50 a year, according to the Treasury.

The move follows a string of cuts to electricity levies over the past year which have shaved about £150 a year off costs.

“For many years, under Conservative governments, policy costs were simply loaded on to household bills through levies,” Healey said. “Today, I am putting an end to that. We’ll introduce a new cost control framework to drive down all aspects of energy bills.”

Healey confirmed he would consider steps to remove standing charges on electricity too, which ​add about £200 a year to the average ​bill. The savings from this measure remain unclear, depending on which costs would move into general taxation and which would be covered through the unit price for electricity.

Healey will continue to alter a subsidy scheme for the UK’s oldest renewable energy projects, around three-quarters of which has been removed from bills and covered by general taxation. The research charity Nesta said this would lower electricity costs by £42 a year.

Healey has scrapped plans for a levy to support hydrogen projects that would otherwise have added £2.60 to £4.50 a year to the average dual-fuel bill.

The government believes that households could save up to £550 a year on energy bills if they invest in solar panels, home batteries and a heat pump. These savings could rise by a further £300 a year with a time-of-use tariff, according to the government.

To help households access these savings, a Warm Home Loans scheme, which launched on Tuesday, will offer government-backed loans of up to £35,000 for low-carbon energy alternatives.

The government said it was committed to rolling out heat pumps through its boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants of up to £7,500 to help meet the £13,600 cost of installing one.

Grants of up to £9,000 a year are available to households that are not connected to the gas grid and rely on high-cost heating oil.

For many, the government’s new measures will come too late to help this winter. But there could be support in the spring from a debt relief scheme.

The government said the delayed scheme will “provide targeted support to customers in genuine financial need”. Total household energy debt has tripled from 2021 to a record £5bn and could reach £7bn by the end of the year .

The one-off, targeted intervention has been designed to help those with debts from the 2022-24 energy crisis and little prospect of repaying them.

Nesta has suggested debt relief could be given to about 2m households for a one-off cost of £2.7bn. This would also cut the £29 a year paid by all households to cover the cost of unpaid bills.

More details on the scheme will follow in early 2027, the government said.
